liturgical_day: Saturday of the Thirty-first Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: You cannot serve God and mammon
theme: Earthly goods are entrusted to us; faithfulness begins with how we use them.
introduction: Jesus asks his disciples to use passing wealth with eternity in view. A small trust reveals whether we are ready for a greater one, and money tests the heart's allegiance. The Fathers connect this teaching to almsgiving without allowing generosity to excuse dishonesty. When the Pharisees mock Jesus, he turns from outward reputation to what God sees within. The question reaches beyond how much we possess: whom do we serve?
hero_alt: Jesus teaches his disciples as a listener shares coins with a poor neighbour, in Byzantine mosaic, blue stained glass and gold leaf.
closing_title: Use what has been entrusted to you
closing: Cyril finds faithfulness in the help we give someone weighed down by sorrow. Ambrose reminds us that wealth neither arrives with us at birth nor accompanies us at death. Bede distinguishes possessing money from serving it. Together, their readings bring the question close to hand: can what we hold today be used freely for another person's need? God knows whether our generosity comes from a faithful heart or from a wish to appear righteous.
copyright_notes: Scripture is an original modernization of the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible, not of USCCB or Vatican News Scripture wording. Patristic insights and expansions are original summaries of the public-domain Newman translation of the Catena Aurea, not verbatim quotations. Mammon retains the traditional term for riches. Verse 9 preserves the Douay-Rheims reading "when you fail", rather than substituting a different textual reading.

verses.text: And I say to you: Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings.
verses.author: St Augustine of Hippo
verses.insight: Almsgiving cannot turn stolen money into an acceptable gift. Augustine calls for generosity from honest labour, with restitution for those we have wronged.
verses.commentary: Augustine warns against reading this command as permission to take another person's goods and give a portion to the poor. Christ the judge cannot be bribed. If we would condemn a human judge who accepted money taken from someone else, we must not imagine God accepting the same bargain. Augustine directs the faithful toward alms from honest work and recalls Zacchaeus, who joined generosity to fourfold restitution. He also explains that earthly wealth is unreliable: it can leave its owner poor, whereas the heart turned toward God possesses a treasure that outward loss cannot take away.
verses.source_label: St Augustine of Hippo, Sermon 113, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:8–13

verses.text: Whoever is faithful in what is least is faithful also in what is greater; and whoever is unjust in what is little is unjust also in what is greater.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril identifies the small trust with earthly wealth. Faithfulness becomes visible when we help people bowed down by sorrow.
verses.commentary: Cyril reads this saying as Christ's answer to the reluctance of those who pursue wealth yet neglect the needy. Earthly possessions are the little thing entrusted to us; to someone who judges by heavenly things, they are small indeed. Faithful use of them means giving help to people burdened by sorrow. The comparison between little and much therefore concerns an actual responsibility, rather than an abstract test of character. Cyril connects our treatment of this lesser trust with our readiness for spiritual gifts, and asks how unfaithfulness here can lead to the true riches of divine grace.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:8–13

verses.text: If, then, you have not been faithful with unjust mammon, who will trust you with what is true?
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: The true riches, in Cyril's reading, are the fruitful gift of divine grace. Money is a lesser trust whose use exposes our willingness to care for others.
verses.commentary: Cyril hears Christ opening the heart's eyes to the difference between earthly possessions and true riches. Money is a small matter beside the gift of divine grace, which bears fruit in the soul and impresses God's image upon it. Yet this lesser trust is not beneath our attention. A person proves faithful in it by helping those who suffer. Cyril's question follows Christ's: if we refuse faithfulness in the goods already entrusted to us, how can we expect the greater gift? His reading holds practical mercy and the soul's reception of grace together.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:8–13

verses.text: And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?
verses.author: St Ambrose of Milan
verses.insight: Wealth is foreign to us: we neither bring it into life nor carry it away. Ambrose calls Christ our own because he is our life.
verses.commentary: Ambrose pauses over the contrast between another's property and what is our own. Riches are external to human nature. They do not come into the world with us, and they do not depart with us when life ends. For that reason he calls them foreign to us, however firmly we may hold them for a time. Christ, by contrast, is ours because he is the life of the human person. Ambrose recalls that Christ came to his own. His reading measures belonging by our relation to Christ rather than by the possessions we temporarily control.
verses.source_label: St Ambrose of Milan, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:8–13

verses.text: No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will hold to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and mammon.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede distinguishes having wealth from serving it. A person freed from its yoke can distribute it instead of standing guard over it as a slave.
verses.commentary: Bede asks the covetous to hear the force of Christ's warning: service to Christ cannot be joined to service to riches. He pays close attention to the word serve. Jesus does not simply condemn the person who has possessions; he exposes the one who has become their servant. Such a person watches over wealth as a slave watches over a master's property. Someone who has thrown off that yoke can instead dispose of possessions freely. Bede's distinction makes the use of wealth a question of allegiance: who governs the person who holds it?
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, drawing on Jerome, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:8–13

verses.text: Now the Pharisees, who were covetous, heard all these things, and they derided him.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: Bede hears their mockery as resistance to mercy and humility. Jesus' teaching challenges both their attachment to gain and their confidence in their own conduct.
verses.commentary: Bede places the mockery after Christ's call to welcome repentant sinners and to practise almsgiving. Instead of boasting about their own righteousness, the Pharisees were being asked to receive others and seek the remedy of mercy themselves. They laughed at the preacher of humility and frugality. Bede suggests two possible reasons: his commands seemed insufficiently profitable to them, or his teaching exposed the excesses of their former conduct. He leaves these as alternatives. In either case, their response shows resistance to a teaching that would change how they regarded both their possessions and themselves.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:14–18

verses.text: And he said to them: You are those who justify yourselves before people, but God knows your hearts; for what is highly esteemed among people is an abomination before God.
verses.author: St Bede the Venerable
verses.insight: An appearance of righteousness can hide contempt for those who need mercy. Bede reminds us that God sees the pride behind that appearance.
verses.commentary: Bede explains self-justification through the way these hearers look at sinners. They treat others as weak and beyond hope while imagining themselves complete, with no need for the remedy of almsgiving. That contrast can sustain a respectable appearance before other people. It cannot conceal the heart from God. Bede describes the pride underneath as deadly and insists that its true depth is known to the one who brings hidden darkness to light. Christ's judgment therefore reaches the inward presumption that human approval may leave untouched: the belief that mercy is for others and unnecessary for oneself.
verses.source_label: St Bede the Venerable, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 16:14–18
